title: The Invention of the Industrial Robot
summary: How American inventor George Devol built the Unimate, the first industrial robot, in the 1950s, taking on dangerous factory work so human workers would not have to risk injury.
poll: The industrial robot is one of the most important inventions ever created for keeping workers safe from dangerous or exhausting jobs.

versions.title: A Machine That Moves Alone
versions.text:
See that robot move. It can do jobs. It does jobs for us.

Some jobs are hard. Some jobs are not safe. A robot can help.

Long ago, there were no real robots. A play told of robots. It was in 1920.

A man made a real robot. His name was Devol. He built a big robot arm.

The arm could lift things. It worked in a car plant. It did not get tired.

This robot was a big step. Many plants then used robots like it.

Now, robots help a lot. Some help in plants. Some help in clinics. Some help in space.

Robots give us new help. They do jobs that are hard or not safe.

versions.title: A Machine That Moves Alone
versions.text:
A robot is a machine. It moves and does jobs on its own, often by following a set plan. A person does not need to do every hard or unsafe task alone.

Long ago, there were no real robots. The word "robot" came from a play written in 1920, in a land far from America. In that play, robots were only an idea. They were not real machines yet.

In the 1950s, an engineer in America built something new. George Devol had spent years designing a big robot arm made of strong metal. He wanted machines to do the hardest, most repeated jobs.

Working with his own idea, Devol built a robot arm that could lift heavy parts again and again. A car plant in America began using it in 1961. It never once grew tired.

This clever invention became a lasting model. Many plants still use robots built on his basic idea, more than sixty years later.

Robots now help in millions of places. Robots help build cars. They help doctors treat patients. They even help explore outer space.

Robots give people new power and real safety. They take on jobs that are hard, slow, or too unsafe for a person.

versions.title: The Invention of the Industrial Robot
versions.text:
A robot is a machine built to move and perform tasks on its own. It usually follows a set plan from a computer. For many workers, a robot is simply the tool that takes on the hardest or most dangerous jobs.

The idea of robots has existed for a long time. Early robots were only fictional. They appeared in stories and plays. They were not real, working machines.

That changed in the 1950s. An American engineer named George Devol had spent years designing a large robot arm. He knew its promise firsthand. He wanted machines to handle the most repetitive, dangerous factory work.

Working hard, Devol built a robot arm made of strong metal. It could lift and move heavy parts again and again. A car plant began using it in 1961, and it never grew tired or complained.

That working design became the model for later robots. Many still follow it today, more than sixty years later.

Today, robots help in millions of workplaces. People rely on robots to build cars, assist in surgery, explore space, and handle materials too dangerous for human hands.

Many modern robots now use cameras and sensors to see their surroundings. Other robots still follow a simple, repeated set of motions.

More than anything, a robot means safety. It takes on the hardest and most dangerous work so people do not have to.

A robot is a machine engineered to move and perform tasks on its own, usually by following a set plan from a computer rather than a person's direct control. For countless workers, a robot is the everyday tool that makes dangerous or exhausting jobs genuinely survivable.

The idea of robots has existed for a long time across many cultures, mostly as fiction rather than fact. Early robots, though, were only imagined, appeared in stories and plays, and were not real, working machines at all.

Everything changed in the 1950s. An American engineer named George Devol unveiled a strikingly different machine. Devol had spent years designing a large robot arm. He understood its promise firsthand. His determination pushed him to design something safer and more reliable for workers.

Working closely with his own idea, Devol built a robot arm made of strong metal. It could lift and move heavy parts again and again, with no risk to a human worker. A car plant began using it in 1961, and it never grew tired, distracted, or injured on the job.

That working design eventually became the basic blueprint for later robots, more than sixty years later, from early bulky arms to today's precise machines.

Today, robots help in millions of workplaces worldwide, giving workers genuine independence from the most punishing tasks. People rely on robots to build cars and assist in surgery. Some explore distant planets or handle materials too dangerous for human hands.

versions.title: The Invention of the Industrial Robot
versions.text:
A robot is a machine engineered to move and perform tasks on its own, usually by following a set plan from a computer rather than a person's direct control. It is designed so dangerous, exhausting, or highly repetitive work no longer has to fall entirely on a human worker.

The idea of robots has existed for a long time across many cultures, mostly as fiction rather than fact. Early records depict imagined machines in ancient myths and later in stories and plays. Those early robots, though, were purely fictional. They were nearly impossible to build with the technology available at the time.

George Devol was born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1912. As a young inventor fascinated by machines and electronics, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem. Factories needed a way to handle repetitive, dangerous tasks without endangering a human worker.

Working largely on his own, Devol experimented with various mechanical arms and simple programmable controls. These had been built mostly for isolated demonstrations, not genuine factory use. He admired the underlying engineering, but no one had yet adapted it to perform real, repeated industrial work.

Devol set out to refine the design, over years of careful experimentation. He built a large robot arm from strong metal, guided by a simple, repeatable program stored on a magnetic drum. He completed his working machine, called the Unimate, and filed a patent describing it in 1954.

That robot arm became one of the first true industrial robots ever built. A car factory in New Jersey installed it in 1961 to lift and stack hot, heavy metal parts.

Today, robots are used worldwide, across dozens of distinct industries, from car factories to hospitals to outer space. Workers depend on robots daily to handle dangerous materials, assist in surgery, and perform tasks requiring tireless precision.

Whichever robot a workplace uses, the basic idea stays the same: a robot should take on dangerous or exhausting work, rather than leaving a person to risk injury alone.

versions.title: The Invention of the Industrial Robot
versions.text:
A robot is a machine engineered to move and perform tasks on its own, precisely following a set plan from a computer rather than a person's direct control, so dangerous or highly repetitive work no longer has to fall entirely on a human worker.

Factories with dangerous or highly repetitive tasks once had essentially no reliable method for protecting workers, which made serious injury an ordinary, expected risk of the job.

George Devol was born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1912. As a young inventor fascinated by machines and electronics, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem. Factories needed a way to handle repetitive, dangerous tasks without endangering a human worker.

While working largely on his own, Devol experimented with various mechanical arms and simple programmable controls. These had been built mostly for isolated demonstrations, not genuine factory use. He admired the underlying engineering, but no one had yet adapted it to perform real, repeated industrial work.

Devol set out to refine the design, over years of careful testing and revision. He built a large robot arm from strong metal, guided by a simple, repeatable program stored on a rotating magnetic drum. He completed his working machine, named the Unimate, and filed a patent describing it in 1954.

This innovative machine eventually became known as one of the first true industrial robots. A car factory in New Jersey installed it in 1961 to lift and stack hot, heavy metal parts, work considered far too dangerous for most human workers.

Today, robots are used worldwide, across dozens of distinct industries, from car factories to hospitals to outer space exploration. Workers depend on robots daily to handle dangerous materials, assist in surgery, and perform tasks requiring tireless precision.

Many modern robots now use cameras, sensors, and small onboard computers rather than fixed mechanical programs, letting a single flexible machine adapt instantly to new tasks without being reprogrammed by hand, something the original Unimate could never have managed on its own.

versions.title: The Invention of the Industrial Robot
versions.text:
A robot is a machine engineered to move and perform tasks on its own, precisely following a set plan from a computer rather than a person's direct control, so dangerous or highly repetitive work no longer has to fall entirely on a human worker, a method so effective that its basic principle remains central to modern manufacturing more than six decades after it was first attempted.

Factories with dangerous or highly repetitive tasks once had essentially no reliable method for protecting workers, which made serious injury an ordinary, expected risk of the job for generations of factory employees and their families.

George Devol was born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1912, the son of a businessman, and as a young inventor fascinated by machines and electronics, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem: handling the most repetitive, dangerous tasks inside a factory without endangering a human worker nearby.

While working largely on his own, Devol experimented with various mechanical arms and simple programmable controls, originally built mostly for isolated demonstrations rather than genuine factory use, and although he admired the underlying engineering, no one had yet adapted it specifically to perform real, repeated industrial work reliably over time.

Devol set out to refine the design considerably, devoting years of careful, painstaking testing and revision to the project, building a large robot arm from strong metal, guided by a simple, repeatable program stored on a rotating magnetic drum, and he completed his working machine, named the Unimate, filing a patent describing it in the historic year of 1954.

This innovative machine eventually became known as one of the first true industrial robots, when a car factory in New Jersey installed it in 1961 to lift and stack hot, heavy metal parts, work considered far too dangerous for most human workers to perform safely for long.

Today, robots are used worldwide, across dozens of distinct industries, from car factories to hospitals to outer space exploration, and workers depend on robots daily to handle dangerous materials, assist in surgery, and perform tasks requiring tireless precision, often now guided by cameras, sensors, and onboard computers rather than fixed mechanical programs alone.

This lasting legacy traces directly back to one largely self-taught American inventor's quiet determination to solve a stubborn safety problem no one else had managed to solve before him, decades before cameras and computers made robots far more flexible than Devol's original Unimate ever was.

Factories with dangerous or highly repetitive tasks once had essentially no reliable method for protecting workers, which made serious injury an ordinary, expected risk of the job for generations of factory employees and their families across many industries.

George Devol was born in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1912, the son of a businessman, and as a young inventor fascinated by machines and electronics, he grew determined to solve one especially stubborn problem: handling the most repetitive, dangerous tasks inside a factory without endangering a human worker nearby on the line.

While working largely on his own, Devol experimented with various mechanical arms and simple programmable controls, originally built mostly for isolated demonstrations rather than genuine factory use, and although he admired the underlying engineering, no one had yet adapted it specifically to perform real, repeated industrial work reliably over time and across shifts.

Devol set out to refine the design considerably, devoting years of careful, painstaking testing and revision to the project, building a large robot arm from strong metal, guided by a simple, repeatable program stored on a rotating magnetic drum, and he completed his working machine, named the Unimate, filing a patent describing it in the historic year of 1954.

This innovative machine eventually became known as one of the first true industrial robots, when a car factory in New Jersey installed it in 1961 to lift and stack hot, heavy metal parts, work considered far too dangerous for most human workers to perform safely for long periods.

Today, robots are used worldwide, across dozens of distinct industries, from car factories to hospitals to outer space exploration, and workers depend on robots daily to handle dangerous materials, assist in surgery, and perform tasks requiring tireless precision, often now guided by cameras, sensors, and onboard computers rather than fixed mechanical programs alone.

This lasting legacy traces directly back to one largely self-taught American inventor's quiet determination to solve a stubborn safety problem that no one else had truly managed to solve before him, decades before cameras, computers, and advanced sensors made robots far more flexible and far safer than Devol's original Unimate ever could have been entirely on its own.

keyWords.example: The old clock relied on a mechanical system of gears to keep time.

keyWords.definition: done the same way over and over again
keyWords.example: The repetitive motion of the assembly line could tire a worker quickly.

keyWords.definition: the work of designing and building machines, structures, or systems
keyWords.example: Her degree in engineering helped her design safer bridges.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of this article?
options: Devol's personal drive to solve a safety problem led to a machine that became the lasting standard
Machines for factory work were never attempted before the twentieth century
Factory injuries have never truly been a problem for most workers
Industrial robots are only useful for professional athletes
questions.why: The article centers on how Devol's determination to solve a stubborn safety problem led to a machine that became the lasting standard.

wrong.B: The article describes earlier fictional robots dating back further.
wrong.C: The article explicitly describes this as a widespread, serious problem for workers.
wrong.D: The article describes many industries beyond athletics.

questions.stem: According to the article, how did Devol's background shape his invention?
options: He had never studied machines or electronics at all
He designed the entire machine purely from distant guesswork
He experimented with mechanical arms built for isolated demonstrations
He had no interest in solving factory problems of any kind
questions.why: The article explains that Devol experimented with mechanical arms and controls originally built for isolated demonstrations, before adapting them for factory use.

wrong.A: The article explicitly describes his fascination with machines and electronics.
wrong.B: The article credits careful experimentation and testing, not distant guesswork.
wrong.D: The article describes his strong determination to solve this exact problem.

questions.stem: What evidence suggests early fictional robots were genuinely different from Devol's machine, not simply undocumented?
options: They were brightly painted and somewhat difficult to clean
They required an unusual amount of natural sunlight to use
They were purely fictional and impossible to build with the technology at the time
They were too small to be printed clearly in any book
questions.why: The article specifically cites the purely fictional, unbuildable nature of early robots as evidence of a real difference from Devol's working machine.

wrong.A: Paint or cleaning is not discussed in the article.
wrong.B: Sunlight is not discussed as a factor for robots.
wrong.D: Printing in books is not the article's framing of early robots.

questions.stem: Why does the article emphasize that Devol devoted years to careful testing and revision?
options: To argue that careful testing was ultimately unnecessary
To prove that building such machines is an unusually dangerous hobby
To show that a reliable, working machine required real effort, not luck
To suggest the final machine ultimately turned out to be a failure
questions.why: Emphasizing years of careful testing highlights that the breakthrough came from deliberate effort rather than chance.

wrong.A: The article clearly values the careful testing process.
wrong.B: Danger as a hobby is not discussed in the article.
wrong.D: The article presents the final machine as a lasting success.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Devol's design spread so widely over the following decades?
options: It was required everywhere by a brand-new international law
No other industrial robot was ever built again after this one
It likely solved a problem that many factories and workers shared
It was only ever used by a small group of professional performers
questions.why: Since the design became the widely followed blueprint, it likely solved a shared problem across many factories and workers.

wrong.A: No such law is mentioned anywhere in the article.
wrong.B: The article describes many robots that still exist today.
wrong.D: The article mentions many industries, not only performance.

questions.stem: In this article, what does the word stubborn most likely mean?
options: Difficult to solve, change, or deal with
Extremely cheerful and easy to please
Brightly colored and easy to spot
Quick to agree with any new idea
questions.why: Stubborn means difficult to solve or deal with, describing the persistent problem of protecting workers from dangerous tasks.

wrong.B: Stubborn does not describe cheerfulness.
wrong.C: Stubborn does not describe color or appearance.
wrong.D: Stubborn is closer to resistant to change, not quick agreement.

questions.stem: How does the article primarily structure its account of the robot's development?
options: By presenting two opposing viewpoints without any real resolution
By comparing several completely unrelated writing systems
By listing a series of unrelated facts about Kentucky generally
By tracing a problem through a specific solution to its lasting modern impact
questions.why: The article moves from the dangers of earlier factory work, to Devol's specific solution, to its continuing influence today.

wrong.A: No opposing viewpoints are presented in the article.
wrong.B: No unrelated writing systems are compared in the article.
wrong.C: The facts connect into one developing story, not an unrelated list.

questions.stem: Based on the article, which outcome most directly resulted from Devol's industrial robot?
options: Teaching quickly became the only career ever open to engineers
All factories everywhere switched entirely to robots within years
Human workers became completely unnecessary in every factory
Millions of workers gained a dependable way to avoid dangerous tasks
questions.why: The article directly credits the robot with giving millions of workers a dependable way to avoid the most dangerous factory tasks.

wrong.A: The article does not claim teaching became the only career available.
wrong.B: An immediate, total switch by all factories is not described.
wrong.C: Human workers are not described as completely unnecessary.

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how the article uses evidence about both the dangers of earlier factory work and Devol's personal determination to explain why his invention became the enduring standard.
checklist: Analyzes the documented dangers of earlier, unprotected factory work
Explains how Devol's engineering background and determination shaped his invention
Connects his work to its lasting influence on workers and industries today
HIGH.modelAnswer: Before the 1950s, factories with dangerous or highly repetitive tasks had essentially no reliable method for protecting workers, making serious injury an ordinary, expected risk of the job. George Devol, an inventor fascinated by machines and electronics, grew determined to solve this stubborn problem after experimenting with mechanical arms originally built for isolated demonstrations. Devoting years to careful, painstaking testing, he built a large robot arm, the Unimate, guided by a simple, repeatable program stored on a magnetic drum. This mechanical design proved reliable enough for genuine industrial work, and it ultimately became the blueprint that factory robots worldwide continue to follow, giving millions of workers a dependable way to avoid the most dangerous and exhausting tasks.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about how the robot arm changed daily life for workers?
options: It likely made dangerous jobs much safer
It likely made dangerous jobs much harder
It had no effect on jobs at all
It only worked outside in the rain
LOW.why: Since the robot arm took on heavy, repeated lifting, it likely made dangerous jobs much safer for workers.

wrong.B: The text shows the robot solved a problem, not created one.
wrong.C: The text clearly shows jobs changed because of the robot.
wrong.D: No outdoor-only limit is mentioned in the story.

LOW.stem: Why is 1961 an important year in this story?
options: It is when a car plant began using Devol's robot
It is when the word "robot" was first written
It is when plants stopped using any tools
It is when phones were first invented
LOW.why: The text says a car plant began using Devol's robot arm in 1961.

wrong.B: The word "robot" came from a play written earlier, in 1920.
wrong.C: Plants stopping tool use is not mentioned.
wrong.D: Phone invention is not discussed in this story.

LOW.stem: Why does the story explain that early robots were only an idea in a play?
options: To show why Devol's real robot was such an important change
To explain how to build a tall house
To describe a different, unrelated invention
To list facts with no connection to each other
LOW.why: Describing the earlier, fictional idea helps readers understand why Devol's real, working robot was such an important change.

wrong.B: Building houses in general is not the topic.
wrong.C: The earlier fictional idea is directly related, not unrelated.
wrong.D: The facts connect to build one clear story.

LOW.stem: What is the effect of the robot arm never getting tired?
options: It could do the same hard job again and again
It could only work for one minute a day
It made the robot arm impossible to use at all
It cost nothing at all to build the robot
LOW.why: The text shows that never getting tired let the robot arm do the same hard job again and again.

wrong.B: The text shows the opposite; it worked all day long.
wrong.C: The robot could clearly be used, as shown in the story.
wrong.D: Cost is not discussed in the story.

MID.stem: What is the most likely reason the article explains that early robots were only fictional?
options: To help readers understand why Devol's robot arm was such an important improvement
To give a full history of plays written in other countries
To compare robots with spoken language in general
To explain how modern phones are built today
MID.why: Describing the earlier, fictional idea helps readers understand just how significant Devol's improvement really was.

wrong.B: Play history in general is not the article's focus.
wrong.C: Spoken language in general is not compared in detail.
wrong.D: Phone construction is not discussed in the article.

MID.stem: If Devol had not spent years designing a large robot arm, what does the article suggest might have happened?
options: He might not have understood the machine's promise as deeply
The machine would have been built in exactly the same way
Nothing about the story would change at all
He would have built the machine using only hand tools
MID.why: Since the article credits his firsthand design experience with his understanding of the machine's promise, skipping that experience might have changed his understanding.

wrong.B: The article implies his experience mattered, so this seems unlikely.
wrong.C: His experience is presented as directly relevant.
wrong.D: The article describes him building a robot arm, not using only hand tools.

MID.stem: How does the article's final paragraph support its main point?
options: It shows the long-term impact that grew out of Devol's design
It introduces an entirely new, unrelated topic
It contradicts facts given earlier in the article
It simply repeats the opening sentence word for word
MID.why: The ending connects Devol's design to its lasting impact on factory safety today, reinforcing the article's main point.

wrong.B: The ending stays on the topic of the design's impact.
wrong.C: The ending supports, rather than contradicts, earlier details.
wrong.D: The ending adds new information about lasting impact, not a repeated sentence.

MID.stem: Which word from the article is closest in meaning to firsthand?
options: Directly experienced
Loudly spoken
Freshly painted
Lightly carried
MID.why: Firsthand means gained through direct personal experience, which is close in meaning to directly experienced.

wrong.B: Loudly spoken describes volume, not personal experience.
wrong.C: Freshly painted describes appearance, not experience.
wrong.D: Lightly carried describes weight, not experience.

HIGH.stem: Which claim would the article most strongly support with evidence?
options: The lasting value of Devol's robot depended on combining engineering skill with years of careful testing
Only factory workers themselves can ever design useful robots
Mechanical farming played the central role in the industrial robot's spread
Devol's robot has remained completely unused since the 1950s
HIGH.why: The article's evidence, that Devol's engineering background combined with years of testing produced the breakthrough, supports the idea that combining skill with careful testing was essential.

wrong.B: The article centers an engineer's study and testing, not a requirement that only factory workers can invent such machines.
wrong.C: Farming is not discussed in this article.
wrong.D: The article states the design is still followed today.

HIGH.stem: What is the most likely reason the article contrasts earlier fictional robots with Devol's working industrial machine?
options: To highlight exactly what made his invention a genuine breakthrough
To argue that factory workers were entirely without hope before the 1950s
To prove that Kentucky invented all robotics technology alone
To suggest the machine was built with no real planning at all
HIGH.why: Contrasting the purely fictional earlier robots with the later working industrial machine highlights precisely what made the breakthrough so meaningful.

wrong.B: The article does not claim workers were entirely without hope, just at risk from unprotected tasks.
wrong.C: The article credits one inventor, not an entire state.
wrong.D: The article describes years of careful testing, not a lack of planning.

HIGH.stem: Based on the article, which best explains why Devol's machine became so influential?
options: It was the first machine to combine mechanical reliability with real, repeated industrial use
It was invented by a government health agency
It replaced the need for any human worker at all
It was the only invention ever created for any industrial purpose
HIGH.why: The article credits the machine's lasting influence to its unprecedented combination of mechanical reliability and real industrial use, which led to widespread adoption.

wrong.B: The article credits one individual inventor, not a government agency.
wrong.C: The article still describes human workers performing other tasks, not being fully replaced.
wrong.D: The article clearly describes it as specific to dangerous, repetitive work.

HIGH.stem: Which word pair from the article are most closely related in meaning?
options: Stubborn and industrial
Firsthand and mechanical
Mechanical and engineering
Workers and Kentucky
HIGH.why: Mechanical describes something relating to machines, and engineering describes the work of designing such machines, so these two words relate closely in meaning, unlike the other mismatched pairs.

wrong.A: Stubborn describes difficulty, while industrial describes factories; these describe different things.
wrong.B: Firsthand describes direct experience, while mechanical describes machines; these describe different things.
wrong.D: Workers are people, while Kentucky is a place; these are different kinds of words.
